solution:
Conductivity \(\kappa\) is defined per unit VOLUME of solution: it is the conductance of a solution held between two electrodes of unit area of cross section placed unit distance apart, since \(G = \dfrac{\kappa A}{l} = \kappa\) when \(A\) and \(l\) are both unity. So what \(\kappa\) measures is the current-carrying ability of ONE unit volume of the solution.

On dilution the same amount of electrolyte is spread through a larger volume, so the number of ions present in each unit volume falls. With fewer charge carriers between the electrodes, the conductance of that unit volume, and hence \(\kappa\), falls.

This holds for strong and weak electrolytes alike, though for different reasons:

For a strong electrolyte dissociation is already complete, so the number of ions furnished per mole does not change on dilution; they are simply thinned out over more volume.

For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) does increase on dilution, so the TOTAL number of ions in the solution increases. Even so the volume increases faster than the ion count, so the number of ions per unit volume still decreases and \(\kappa\) still falls.

Contrast this with molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}\), which INCREASES on dilution. \(\Lambda_m\) counts all the ions supplied by one mole of electrolyte, no matter how large the volume \(V\) they occupy, so the fall in \(\kappa\) is more than compensated by the rise in \(V\). The two quantities move in opposite directions precisely because one is defined per unit volume and the other per mole.

Conductivity decreases with dilution because it is a per-unit-volume quantity, and dilution reduces the number of current-carrying ions contained in each unit volume of the solution.

Water is an extremely weak electrolyte: it self-ionises only to a minute extent,

\(\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-}\)

Because of this, \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for water cannot be found by the method used for strong electrolytes. For a strong electrolyte \(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\) is linear and the intercept at \(c^{1/2} \to 0\) gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\); for water the plot rises steeply near infinite dilution and is not linear, and the conductivity at such low concentration is far too small to be measured accurately. Extrapolation is therefore not available.

The way to determine it is Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, which states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the independent contributions of its cation and anion. For water,

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\text{H}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\text{OH}^{-})\)

The two ionic values are obtained from STRONG electrolytes, whose \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) is measurable by extrapolation. Take \(\text{HCl}\), \(\text{NaOH}\) and \(\text{NaCl}\) and combine them as

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaOH}) - \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaCl})\)

This works because the unwanted ions cancel:

\((\lambda_{\text{H}^{+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{\circ}) + (\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{\circ}) - (\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{\circ}) = \lambda_{\text{H}^{+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{\circ}\)

Using the ionic values at \(298\,\text{K}\), \(\lambda^{\circ}(\text{H}^{+}) = 349.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\lambda^{\circ}(\text{OH}^{-}) = 199.1\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\):

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = (349.6 + 199.1)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Determine it indirectly, by Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, as \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaOH}) - \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaCl}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\text{H}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\text{OH}^{-}) = 548.7\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).

Methanoic acid, \(\text{HCOOH}\), is a weak electrolyte, so its limiting molar conductivity cannot be got by extrapolation and must come from Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{HCOOH}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\text{H}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\text{HCOO}^{-})\)

\(= (349.6 + 54.6)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 404.2\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

The degree of dissociation at concentration \(c\) is the ratio of the molar conductivity at that concentration to the limiting value:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{46.1\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}{404.2\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}} = 0.1141\)

For the equilibrium \(\text{HCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{HCOO}^{-}\), Ostwald's dilution law gives the dissociation constant. The full expression is kept here, the \((1-\alpha)\) denominator is NOT approximated to 1, since \(\alpha\) is over 11 per cent and dropping it would raise \(K_a\) by about 13 per cent:

\(K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha} = \dfrac{0.025\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times (0.1141)^{2}}{1 - 0.1141}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.025 \times 0.01302}{0.8859}\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = \dfrac{3.255 \times 10^{-4}}{0.8859}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(= 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Degree of dissociation \(\alpha = 0.114\) (about 11.4 per cent); dissociation constant \(K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

Conductivity. The resistance of a column of solution of length \(l\) and area of cross section \(A\) is \(R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}\), where \(\rho\) is the resistivity. Conductivity \(\kappa\) is the reciprocal of resistivity, \(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho}\). Since the conductance is \(G = \dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{\kappa A}{l}\), putting \(A = 1\) and \(l = 1\) gives \(G = \kappa\). So conductivity is the conductance of ONE UNIT VOLUME of solution held between two electrodes of unit area of cross section placed unit distance apart. Its SI unit is \(\text{S m}^{-1}\); it is often quoted in \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\).

Molar conductivity. \(\Lambda_m\) is the conductance of the volume \(V\) of solution that contains ONE MOLE of electrolyte, kept between two electrodes unit distance apart and of area large enough to hold that whole volume:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \kappa V\)

Its SI unit is \(\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). In practical units, with \(\kappa\) in \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and \(c\) in \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\), a factor of \(1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) is needed to make the volume basis consistent:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\,(\text{S cm}^{-1}) \times 1000\,(\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1})}{c\,(\text{mol L}^{-1})}\), giving \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Variation with concentration.

Conductivity: \(\kappa\) DECREASES as the solution is diluted, for both strong and weak electrolytes. It is a per-unit-volume quantity, and on dilution the same electrolyte is spread through more volume, so the number of ions available to carry current in each unit volume falls.

Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_m\) INCREASES on dilution, for both types. It counts all the ions supplied by one mole, however large the volume they occupy, and the decrease in \(\kappa\) is more than compensated by the increase in \(V\). The two therefore move in opposite directions.

The MANNER of the increase in \(\Lambda_m\) differs sharply between the two types, and this is the diagnostic difference:

Strong electrolytes (for example \(\text{KCl}\), \(\text{NaCl}\)) are completely dissociated at all concentrations, so the number of ions per mole is essentially fixed. \(\Lambda_m\) rises only slowly on dilution, and the rise is due to weakening inter-ionic attraction, the ionic atmosphere exerting smaller relaxation and electrophoretic drag as the ions move further apart. The variation is linear in \(c^{1/2}\):

\(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\)

A plot of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(c^{1/2}\) is a straight line of slope \(-A\) whose intercept at \(c^{1/2} = 0\) gives the limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\). The constant \(A\) depends on the charge type of the electrolyte, so all 1-1 electrolytes share one value, all 2-1 electrolytes another, and so on.

Weak electrolytes (for example \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)) are only slightly dissociated at ordinary concentrations, so \(\Lambda_m\) is low there. On dilution the degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) rises, the number of ions furnished by one mole increases, and \(\Lambda_m\) rises steeply near infinite dilution. The plot against \(c^{1/2}\) is a curve, not a straight line, so \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) CANNOT be found by extrapolation; at concentrations low enough for \(\alpha \to 1\) the conductivity is too small to measure accurately. \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) is instead obtained from Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, and the ratio

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}}\)

then gives the degree of dissociation at any concentration.

Conductivity \(\kappa\) is the conductance of unit volume of solution and decreases on dilution for all electrolytes; molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m = \kappa/c\) is the conductance of the solution containing one mole and increases on dilution for all electrolytes, slowly and linearly in \(c^{1/2}\) for strong electrolytes but steeply and non-linearly for weak ones.

Molar conductivity is the conductivity divided by the concentration, \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}\). The two quantities as given are on different volume bases, \(\kappa\) is per \(\text{cm}^{3}\) and \(c\) is per litre, so a factor of \(1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) is needed to make them consistent:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\,(\text{S cm}^{-1}) \times 1000\,(\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1})}{c\,(\text{mol L}^{-1})}\)

Substituting \(\kappa = 0.0248\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and \(c = 0.20\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\):

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{0.0248\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.20\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = \dfrac{24.8}{0.20}\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

The same result in SI units, with \(\kappa = 2.48\,\text{S m}^{-1}\) and \(c = 200\,\text{mol m}^{-3}\), is \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{2.48}{200} = 1.24 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), which is the same value since \(1\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 10^{4}\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).

\(\Lambda_m = 124\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) (that is, \(1.24 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)).

The cell constant \(G^{*}\) is the ratio \(\dfrac{l}{A}\) of the conductivity cell, fixed by its geometry. Conductance and conductivity are related by \(\kappa = G \times G^{*} = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R}\), so

\(G^{*} = \kappa R\)

Substituting \(\kappa = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and \(R = 1500\,\Omega\):

\(G^{*} = 0.146 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1500\,\Omega\)

\(= 0.219\,\text{cm}^{-1}\)

The unit works out as \(\text{cm}^{-1}\) because \(\text{S} \times \Omega = 1\), siemens being the reciprocal of the ohm. In SI units the same cell constant is \(21.9\,\text{m}^{-1}\).

Cell constant \(G^{*} = 0.219\,\text{cm}^{-1}\) (equivalently \(21.9\,\text{m}^{-1}\)).

The table heads its second row \(10^{2} \times \kappa/\text{S m}^{-1}\), so the tabulated numbers are \(100\) times the conductivity IN SI UNITS. Reading the header literally, for \(c = 0.001\,\text{M}\) the entry \(1.237\) means \(10^{2}\kappa = 1.237\), that is \(\kappa = 1.237 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S m}^{-1}\), and NOT \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\). Working throughout in SI avoids a factor-of-1000 slip: express the concentration in \(\text{mol m}^{-3}\) using \(1\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = 1000\,\text{mol m}^{-3}\), and then

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\,(\text{S m}^{-1})}{c\,(\text{mol m}^{-3})}\), giving \(\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Finally convert with \(1\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 10^{4}\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).

For the first row: \(\kappa = 1.237 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S m}^{-1}\), \(c = 1\,\text{mol m}^{-3}\), so \(\Lambda_m = 1.237 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 123.7\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Repeating for every row, and taking square roots of the concentrations for the plot:

| \(c/\text{mol L}^{-1}\) | \(c^{1/2}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\) | \(\kappa/\text{S m}^{-1}\) | \(\Lambda_m/\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.001 | 0.0316 | 0.01237 | 123.7 |
| 0.010 | 0.1000 | 0.1185 | 118.5 |
| 0.020 | 0.1414 | 0.2315 | 115.75 |
| 0.050 | 0.2236 | 0.5553 | 111.06 |
| 0.100 | 0.3162 | 1.0674 | 106.74 |

The plot. Plotting \(\Lambda_m\) on the \(y\)-axis against \(c^{1/2}\) on the \(x\)-axis gives points that fall close to a descending straight line: \(\Lambda_m\) drops steadily from \(123.7\) to \(106.74\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) as \(c^{1/2}\) rises from \(0.0316\) to \(0.3162\). This is the behaviour expected of a strong 1-1 electrolyte, described by the Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation

\(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - Ac^{1/2}\)

so the intercept at \(c^{1/2} = 0\) is \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) and the slope is \(-A\).

The extrapolation. Fitting a least-squares straight line through all five points gives

\(\text{slope} = -59.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\), \(\text{intercept} = \Lambda_m^{\circ} = 124.7\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

The residuals about this line run \(+0.82, -0.34, -0.65, -0.49, +0.66\), a systematic curvature rather than random scatter. That is expected: the equation above is a LIMITING law, strictly valid only at low concentration, and the two most concentrated points (\(0.05\) and \(0.10\,\text{M}\)) lie outside its range and pull the intercept down. Fitting only the three most dilute points, where the law holds best, gives a steeper line and a higher intercept, \(\Lambda_m^{\circ} \approx 126\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). This is the more reliable estimate, and it is corroborated independently by Kohlrausch's law, \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaCl}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\text{Na}^{+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\text{Cl}^{-}) = 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).

\(\Lambda_m\) at the five concentrations \(0.001, 0.010, 0.020, 0.050, 0.100\,\text{M}\) is \(123.7,\ 118.5,\ 115.75,\ 111.06,\ 106.74\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) respectively; the plot of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(c^{1/2}\) is a descending straight line, and its intercept gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\text{NaCl}) \approx 124.7\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) from all five points, rising to about \(126\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) if only the dilute points are used.
_note: The intercept depends on which points are fitted, so the method is stated explicitly. Least squares on all five points gives 124.7; on the three most dilute points it gives 125.9 and on the two most dilute 126.1. The residual pattern (+,-,-,-,+) about the five-point line shows real curvature, i.e. the two most concentrated points lie outside the range of the Debye-Huckel-Onsager limiting law. The dilute-only value agrees with the chapter's own Kohlrausch figure for NaCl (50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4, Table 2.4, also quoted as 126.4 in Example 2.8), which is an independent check. I have led with the all-points value because that is what the question as worded asks for (plot the given data, read the intercept), and flagged the refinement. If the printed key differs it is most likely because it fits a different subset of the points, not because of a method or unit error. I did not open the answer key.

solution:
First the molar conductivity. The conductivity is per \(\text{cm}^{3}\) and the concentration per litre, so the factor \(1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) is needed to put them on the same volume basis:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\,(\text{S cm}^{-1}) \times 1000\,(\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1})}{c\,(\text{mol L}^{-1})} = \dfrac{7.896 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.00241\,\text{mol L}^{-1}}\)

\(= \dfrac{7.896 \times 10^{-2}}{2.41 \times 10^{-3}}\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 32.76\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, so its degree of dissociation at this concentration is the ratio of the measured molar conductivity to the limiting value:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{32.76\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}{390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}} = 0.08390\)

For \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^{-}\), Ostwald's dilution law gives the dissociation constant. The \((1-\alpha)\) denominator is retained rather than approximated to 1:

\(K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha} = \dfrac{0.00241\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times (0.08390)^{2}}{1 - 0.08390}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.00241 \times 7.039 \times 10^{-3}}{0.9161}\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = \dfrac{1.696 \times 10^{-5}}{0.9161}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(= 1.85 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m = 32.76\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\); dissociation constant \(K_a = 1.85 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).
